title: Cold open — do you have to pick a plugin?
text: Someone wondered if you install several plugins, do you have to tell Claude which one to use? You don't. Claude reads the request and reaches for whatever fits. Here's how the stack actually works. First, how the stack actually works. The

title: Act I — how the stack works
text: Natural guess is that you pick a plugin for each task by hand. You don't. With several active, Claude infers from context. The whole stack is available at once, and the request itself decides which layers wake up. Ask a marketing question, the marketing skills switch on. Ask a sales question next, the sales plugin engages. You change the subject, Claude changes tools. No announcement required. Ask something that spans both, and both contribute. Claude coordinates across the domains into one coherent answer, even though several specialized skill sets built it behind the scenes. For a solo operator, that feels less like software and more like a bench of specialists on call. A whole team's coverage, answering in a single voice. And if you want a specific mix, you can just name it. Look at this from a

title: Act II — research into marketing
text: Marketing and a sales angle, and Claude applies both frameworks on purpose, instead of you hoping it guesses. The first handoff, research into marketing. Say you're launching a new service and want positioning grounded in reality, not guesswork. First, the research skills survey the landscape. Who else is out there? How they position, and where the gaps sit. Then those findings hand off to marketing, which builds positioning into the exact gaps the research just found. Value propositions and differentiators aimed at open ground. The result is a stance that stands apart instead of blending in. Distinct, not another me-too voice in a crowded market. Alone, research hands you intelligence and marketing hands you messaging, but messaging with nothing under it. Together, the message is grounded. That's the difference between strategic

title: Act III — research into a sales meeting
text: And generic. The same handoff aimed at a meeting. You've got a meeting with a prospect, and you want to walk in better prepared than anyone they've talked to. Research digs the background, what they build, who their customers are, recent signals. Sales turns it into a brief, your angle, the objections to expect, and what to lead with. Under it, research produces the raw signals, recent news, hiring patterns, competitive position, and sales translates each signal into a move. Intelligence you actually know how to use. A brief without research is surface prep. Research without sales framing is intelligence you can't act on. Together, you understand both their world and your opening within it. title: Act IV — data and support close the loop
text: Marketing builds next quarter's calendar around what actually moved the needle. Support into product, the support skills mine your tickets for the pain that hits the most people hardest. Product turns the top three into buildable specs. You build against documented need. It's the shift from building what feels cool or planning what you enjoy making to working directly against what the evidence in front of you already says. Without the data, a solo operator plans on instinct. With it, creative energy points at the work that actually performs the same effort aimed better. Both handoffs share one shape, measurement feeds making. Data feeds the calendar, support feeds the roadmap, the loop between what customers do and what you build finally closes. title: Act V — the highest-stakes hand-off: a contract
text: Once. Sales pulls up the whole relationship, prior conversations, the deal context. Legal reviews the terms against its risk frameworks. Legal flags the clauses that are unusual for a deal this size. Sales frames the leverage you hold. The two merge into a single negotiation brief, what to push on, what's standard, and where you're strong. You sit down understanding both the commercial relationship and the contractual fine print at the same time, negotiating from complete awareness instead of half of it. Contract review in isolation misses the business context. Sales prep with no legal eye misses the risk stacked. Neither blind spot survives. One rule holds the whole stack together. title: Act VI — keeping combinations sharp
text: Gaps. When a two-plugin flow keeps earning its keep, prospect research into outreach, say write it down. Better, capture the whole workflow as a custom plug-in, so it runs from a single command. One flag, this next part is a forward read, not a settled fact. When you wish a combination could do something it can't, data flowing straight into the road map, that's not a dead end. It's a signal. The integration points are still being built. One plug-in is a specialist. A stack with every handoff intentional is a coordinated team. Your turn. Here's the prompt. Read it with me. I'm about to make a real move, a launch, a pitch, or a build. title: Carry-out + your turn
text: Matter. Then hand those findings to marketing to build positioning into the gaps you found. At the end, show me exactly where the combined answer beats either angle working alone. Name the two domains. Watch the handoff happen, and you'll feel the stack do what no single plug-in could. Clawed in concert. Lay 'em in for bear.
